title: Estimate the Percent of a Number
contentObjective: I can estimate the percent of a number using benchmark percents, rounding, and compatible numbers.
languageObjective: I can explain an estimate using the words about, benchmark, and compatible numbers.

noticeAndWonder.context: A phone's storage screen shows a bar nearly full: 6 GB total, with photos taking the biggest colored stripe and small slivers for mail, messages, and documents.
noticeStarters: I notice the bar is about ___ full.

vocabulary.definition: A reasoned answer that is close enough to be useful, found without exact computation.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una respuesta razonada, lo bastante cercana para ser útil, sin cálculo exacto.
vocabulary.example: 8.6% of 216 is about 10% of 220, which is 22.

vocabulary.definition: A friendly percent — 1%, 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100% — used as a landmark for estimating.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un porcentaje amigable — 1%, 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100% — que sirve de punto de referencia.
vocabulary.example: 4 GB of 6 GB sits between the 50% and 75% marks.

vocabulary.definition: Numbers close to the originals that are easy to compute with mentally.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Números cercanos a los originales con los que es fácil calcular mentalmente.

vocabulary.definition: Two parallel number lines that pair amounts with their percents at the same positions.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Dos rectas paralelas que emparejan cantidades con sus porcentajes en las mismas posiciones.
vocabulary.example: GB on top, percent on the bottom: 1.5 GB lines up with 25%.

vocabulary.definition: The quantity that counts as 100% in a problem — and it can change between questions.
vocabulary.definitionEs: La cantidad que representa el 100% en un problema, y puede cambiar entre preguntas.
vocabulary.example: First the whole is 6 GB; for the photos question the whole becomes the 4 GB used.

launch.narrative: Margaret checked the cloud storage on her phone: 6 GB total, 4 GB used. Approximately what percent of her storage is used — and of the used storage, approximately what percent are photos?

conceptIntro.heading: Approximately — the problem is asking for an estimate
conceptIntro.intro: The word approximately tells you an exact answer is not required. Benchmarks, rounding and compatible numbers get you close, fast.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: Anchor the whole at 100%, mark benchmark percents, and place the amount between the landmarks it falls beside.

iDo.title: Watch me set up the double number line
lines: The whole is 6 GB — that is 100%.
I mark the bottom line in benchmark jumps of 25%: 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100%.
Equivalent ratios give the top line: 25% of 6 GB is 1.5 GB, so the top reads 0, 1.5, 3, 4.5, 6.
4 GB used lands between 4.5 (75%) and 3 (50%), close to 4.5 — so about 70% of the storage is used.

weDo.title: Let's estimate the metal recycling together
lines: The Green-Team recycled 216 pounds of material; 8.6% was metal.
Round both: 8.6% is about 10%, and 216 is about 220.
Compatible numbers work too: 10% of 200 = 20. Both estimates agree — around 20 pounds.

youDo.title: Now you try
lines: Estimate 24% of 81 using a benchmark. Say which benchmark you chose and why.
Then check: is your estimate a little high or a little low?

explore.label: Sort each estimation move: is it using a BENCHMARK PERCENT or COMPATIBLE NUMBERS?

cards.text: Treating 24% as 25% because quarters are easy
Changing 216 pounds to 200 pounds to divide easily
Using 10% of a number and scaling from there
Placing 4 GB between the 50% and 75% marks

explore.instructions: Sort all six, then tell a partner one estimate where you would use BOTH moves at once.

connect.scenario: Margaret's storage: 6 GB total, 4 GB used, and 3.5 GB of the used space is photos. The rest of the used space is mail, messages, and documents.
connect.promptQuestion: Of the USED storage, approximately what percent are photos — and why does the whole change from 6 GB to 4 GB for this question?
connect.prompt: Estimate the percent of used storage that is photos. Name the whole you used and the benchmark you compared against.
connect.check: The whole for this question is 4 GB (100% of the USED storage). 3.5 of 4 GB sits between the 75% benchmark (3 GB) and 100% (4 GB), closer to 100% — about 87%.
connect.modelAnswer: For this question the whole is 4 GB, because we are asked about the used storage — the 6 GB total does not matter now. On a double number line for 4 GB, 75% is 3 GB and 100% is 4 GB. Photos take 3.5 GB, halfway between those marks, so photos are about 87% of the used storage.

approaching.stem: Margaret's phone has 6 GB of storage and 4 GB is used. About what percent is used?
approaching.explanation: 4 out of 6 is 2/3, which is about 67%, so 'about 70%' is the reasonable estimate.
choiceFeedback: That reads the 4 GB as 40% — but the whole is 6, not 10.
25% of 6 GB would be only 1.5 GB.
More than 100% would mean using more storage than the phone has.
hints: 4 out of 6 is the same as 2 out of 3.
Two-thirds is close to which benchmark?

approaching.stem: On the double number line for 6 GB, what amount lines up with 25%?
approaching.explanation: 25% of 6 GB is one quarter of 6, which is 1.5 GB.
choiceFeedback: 2.5 GB would be more than a third of the storage.
That divides 6 by 4.8 rather than by 4.
4 GB lines up near 67%, not 25%.

approaching.stem: Which benchmark percents make good landmarks on a number line?
approaching.explanation: Multiples of 25 (and 10) are friendly landmarks because their amounts are easy to compute.
choiceFeedback: Those percents are no easier to compute with than the original problem.
50% alone leaves most of the line unmarked.
100% alone gives you nothing to compare against in the middle.
hints: Which percents can you find mentally?
Quarters and tenths are the friendly ones.

approaching.stem: To estimate 8.6% of 216 by rounding, which numbers should you use?
approaching.explanation: 8.6% rounds to 10% and 216 rounds to 220 — both are close to the originals and easy to compute.
choiceFeedback: 300 is far from 216, so the estimate drifts too far.
86% misplaces the decimal — that is ten times too large.
1% is far below 8.6%, so the estimate would be far too small.
hints: Round each number to something friendly.
216 is close to which round number?

choiceFeedback: That moves the decimal two places instead of one.
That is 100% of 220, not 10%.
That is 20% of 220.

approaching.stem: The word 'approximately' appears in the storage problem. What does it tell you about the answer you need?
approaching.modelAnswer: It tells me an exact answer is not required — I can use benchmarks and rounding to get close, and 'about 70%' counts as correct.
sentenceStems: So instead of computing exactly, I can ___ .

onLevel.stem: The Green-Team recycled 216 pounds; 8.6% was metal. Using compatible numbers 10% and 200, the estimate is:
choiceFeedback: That is 1% of 200 — the decimal moved one place too far.
That subtracts 8 from 216 instead of taking a percent.
That reads 8.6% as 86 pounds.

onLevel.stem: Photos use 3.5 GB of the 4 GB of used storage. About what percent of the USED storage is photos?
onLevel.explanation: The whole is 4 GB here. 75% of 4 is 3 GB and 100% is 4 GB; 3.5 sits midway — about 87%.
choiceFeedback: That uses 6 GB as the whole, but the question asks about the USED storage.
That reads 3.5 GB as 35% — the whole is 4, not 10.
3.5 out of 4 is clearly below 100%, but not that close to it.
hints: What is the whole for THIS question?
3.5 of 4 is between the 75% and 100% marks.

onLevel.stem: Why did the whole change between the two storage questions?
choices: The second question asks about the used storage, so 4 GB becomes 100%
The phone gained storage between the questions
The whole never changes in a percent problem
Because photos are more important than mail
onLevel.explanation: Each percent question defines its own whole. 'Of the used storage' makes the 4 GB the new 100%.
choiceFeedback: The phone's capacity never changed — the QUESTION changed.
The whole is set by the question, and this pair of questions sets it differently.
Importance has nothing to do with which quantity is the whole.
hints: Which quantity is that question about?

onLevel.explanation: 24% is about 25%, and 81 is about 80. One quarter of 80 is 20.
choiceFeedback: 40 would be about half of 81, but 24% is about a quarter.
8 is about 10% of 81, not 24%.
2 is about 2.5% of 81 — far below 24%.

onLevel.stem: Your estimate for 8.6% of 216 was 22 pounds (using 10% of 220). Is the exact answer higher or lower than 22?
choices: Lower, because both 10% and 220 rounded UP
Higher, because rounding always shrinks the answer
onLevel.explanation: 8.6% went up to 10% and 216 went up to 220, so the estimate overshoots — the exact answer (about 18.6) is lower.
choiceFeedback: Rounding can push an estimate either way; here both pushes were upward.
Exactness is what we gave up when we rounded.
You CAN tell, by looking at which direction each rounding moved.
hints: Which way did each number round?
So the estimate is a little high.

onLevel.stem: Estimate 47% of 312. Show which strategy you used — benchmark, rounding, or compatible numbers — and give your estimate.
onLevel.modelAnswer: 47% is about 50%, and 312 is about 300. Half of 300 is 150, so 47% of 312 is about 150. I used a benchmark (50%) with a compatible number (300).

onLevel.stem: 1 MB equals 0.001 GB. Mail uses 300 MB. About what percent of Margaret's 6 GB is mail?
onLevel.explanation: 300 MB is 0.3 GB. 0.3 of 6 is 0.05, which is 5%.
choiceFeedback: That misplaces the decimal — 50% would be 3 GB, ten times the mail.
0.5% of 6 GB would be only 0.03 GB.
30% of 6 GB would be 1.8 GB, six times the mail.

extending.stem: Two students estimate 8.6% of 216. Ana uses 10% of 220 = 22. Ben uses 10% of 200 = 20. Whose estimate is closer to the exact answer, 18.576?
choices: Ben's — 20 is 1.4 away; Ana's 22 is 3.4 away
extending.explanation: Exact is 18.576. Ben's 20 misses by about 1.4; Ana's 22 misses by about 3.4. Compatible numbers won this one.
choiceFeedback: 22 − 18.576 = 3.424, which is farther than Ben's 1.424.
The two distances are 1.4 and 3.4 — not equal.
Both are valid estimates; the question is which lands closer.

extending.stem: For which problem is ESTIMATING clearly the right tool, rather than exact computation?
choices: Deciding if a $58 jacket at 25% off fits your $45 budget
Programming a bank to compute interest on every account
extending.explanation: A quick benchmark — 25% of 60 is 15, so about $43 — answers the budget question; the others need exactness.
choiceFeedback: Bank interest must be computed exactly, to the cent.
Medicine doses can never be 'about right'.
Test scoring has to be exact for every student.
hints: Money decisions you make in an aisle are estimates.
The other three carry real risk if inexact.

extending.stem: Write your own estimation problem about percent, using a real situation from your life. Then solve it with a benchmark and say whether your estimate runs high or low.
extending.modelAnswer: My playlist has 62 songs and about 48% are hip-hop. 48% is about 50%, and 62 is about 60, so about 30 songs. Both roundings moved in opposite directions, so my estimate is very close.
sentenceStems: ___% is near the benchmark ___ , so my estimate is ___ .

extending.stem: A store marks a $79.95 item 32% off. Which mental estimate best checks the discount?
choices: About one third of 80, so about $26 off
extending.explanation: 32% is near the benchmark 1/3, and $79.95 is nearly 80. A third of 80 is about 26.7.
choiceFeedback: Percent is not a dollar count — 32% of 80 is not automatically $32 (though here it lands nearby, the reasoning is wrong).
That is 4% of 80, a misplaced decimal.
Half would be 50%, far above 32%.

extending.stem: Margaret wants to know what percent of her TOTAL 6 GB is photos (photos = 3.5 GB). Estimate it, and explain why this answer differs from the 87% found earlier.
extending.modelAnswer: 3.5 of 6 GB: 50% of 6 is 3 and 75% is 4.5, so 3.5 GB is about 58% of the total. Earlier the whole was only the 4 GB used, so the same photos were a larger share — 87% of a smaller whole.
sentenceStems: Using 6 GB as the whole, photos are about ___ .
The two answers differ because the whole ___ .

practice.commonMistake: Keeping the same whole for every question — when the problem says 'of the used storage,' the whole changes from 6 GB to 4 GB, and estimates anchored to the old whole are wrong before any arithmetic happens.

exitTicket.stem: Estimate 19% of 412 using benchmarks or compatible numbers.
exitTicket.explanation: 19% is about 20%, and 412 is about 400. 20% of 400 is 0.2 × 400 = 80.
